big_idea: A SPINNER with bigger sections is MORE LIKELY to land there.
learning_intention: We are learning to predict spinner outcomes.
student_learning_goal: I can predict spinner outcomes using likelihood.
success_criteria: I can predict the MOST LIKELY outcome.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Lucky and Mae — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.

minds_on.hook: Lucky: Look at this spinner — RED is the BIG section, BLUE is small. Predict the spin — most likely RED! Lucky opens: 'BIG section, BIG chance — small section, small chance!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Lucky and Mae puppets. 'Friends — yesterday complementary events. Today SPINNERS.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write SPINNER on chart. 'Spinner = a pointer on a circle divided into sections. Bigger section = more likely.'

Demo. Show a spinner with 3/4 red + 1/4 blue. 'Red is BIGGER. Spin — most likely RED.' Spin. Show outcome.

Another spinner: 4 equal quadrants (red, blue, green, yellow). 'All EQUAL — any colour equally likely.'

Another: 1/2 red, 1/4 blue, 1/4 green. 'Red biggest = most likely.'

'Lucky says — bigger section = HIGHER chance. Predict the BIGGEST section first.'

More examples (complementary):
- 1/2 red, 1/2 blue. 'Either red or blue — equal chance. Complementary.'
- 3/4 dog, 1/4 cat. 'Most likely DOG.'
- 1/4 hockey, 1/4 soccer, 1/4 baseball, 1/4 football. 'All equal.'

'Today YOU spin and predict.'

steps.instruction: Whole group: predict 4 spinners' most likely outcomes.
Three stations. A: Use a 2-section spinner; predict + spin 5 times. B: 4-section equal spinner; predict + spin. C: Make your own spinner; predict.
Stretch at C: design a 3-colour spinner with one big section.

steps.teacher_prompt: Show: equal = any colour. Unequal = biggest most likely.

steps.instruction: STRATEGY COMPARE: After Station A, two pairs share HOW they decided which section was 'biggest' — by eye, by counting equal slices, by overlay. Class debates which is most reliable. Cite Bryant & Nunes (2012) — proportional reasoning supports likelihood prediction.
steps.teacher_prompt: Lucky: 'Different paths to find the biggest. The CLEAREST path uses COUNTING.'

differentiation.for_movement_learners: Children physically spin a large floor spinner. NO-PAPER VERSION: clock-spin — child stands, points arm like a clock hand, closes eyes, partner says STOP, child names where their arm lands. Body becomes the spinner.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: reads spinner; predicts most likely; records.

discussion_prompts: What if all sections are equal?
consolidation.exit_routine: Lucky's spinner refrain — Lucky calls 'BIG section, BIG chance —' Class: 'small section, small chance!' (3x with hand gesture). Each child names ONE spinner section and predicts how often the arrow lands there.

assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 3 captures D2.1 + intro to D2.2.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child predicts the SMALLEST section — repairing the small-section trap at Grade 2
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On spinner-section reasoning, the trap is treating ALL sections as equiprobable regardless of size (Fischbein 1975, equiprobability bias). Bryant & Nunes (2012, 'Children's Understanding of Probability') frame proportional reasoning as the prerequisite — 'bigger section = more likely' is proportional-thinking-on-a-circle, the Grade-2 entry to formal probability.

Yesterday's complement work primed the framing. Today the spinner makes proportions VISIBLE. Lesson 4 dice; Lesson 5 mode capstone.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair at A. Spinner has 3/4 red, 1/4 blue. Child predicts BLUE.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'You picked BLUE. But look — RED is the BIGGER section. Lucky says — bigger = more likely.'

Guide. 'Spin many times. Most spins will land RED. So predict RED.'

Roll several times. Child sees most are red. 'See!'

Generlise. 'Lucky says — predict the BIGGEST section.'

If still picking small: provide visual aid showing 'big section vs small section' with arrows.
common_misconceptions: All sections equal regardless of size. (Repair: visual size matters.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child says all sections equally likely: physical demo with a clearly skewed spinner (1 big, 5 small); child predicts where the arrow lands MOST OFTEN over 10 spins.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child can identify biggest section but doesn't connect to likelihood: drill 'BIG section = BIG chance' (Lucky refrain); child re-says before predicting.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child predicts but cannot articulate proportion: use a counted-section spinner (4 of 8 = HALF); child says 'half the spinner means half the chance.'

parts_outline.task: Design your own spinner with one BIG section.
